---
title: "Predictive Bands: Noise & Ensembles"
---



So far we propagated uncertainty in the *inputs* — sample the joint, push it
through ([Chapter 3](03-noise-and-propagation.qmd)).  Predictive uncertainty is
the same move for a **prediction** $\hat y = f(x)$: ask what you don't know, then
estimate it by *sampling* — no posteriors, no variational inference.

## Two Questions, Two Tools

$$
\text{predictive variance} =
\underbrace{\text{aleatoric}}_{\text{data noise}} +
\underbrace{\text{epistemic}}_{\text{model uncertainty}}
$$

They answer different questions, so we build them separately:

- **Aleatoric** — *how noisy is the world here?*  Fit the mean, then **predict the
  noise** $\sigma(x)$ from the residuals.  Irreducible: more data will not shrink it.
- **Epistemic** — *has the model seen data here?*  Fit several models on resampled
  data; their **disagreement** is the uncertainty, and it shrinks as data grows.

A fully Bayesian network is the principled limit — a posterior
$p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)$ that you integrate over.  A **deep ensemble** is the
cheap, well-calibrated stand-in (and a residual model handles the noise); same
answer, far less machinery.  The Bayesian primitives live in
[pyrox](https://github.com/jejjohnson/pyrox) if you want the formal version.

## Aleatoric · Predict the Noise

Fit a mean $f(x)$ and the **residuals are the noise**.  A single error bar assumes
that noise is *constant* — but when it varies, one bar is too wide in the calm
regions and too narrow in the loud ones.  The fix: fit a *second* model to the
**squared residuals**, giving a noise level $\sigma(x)$, and band with
$f(x)\pm 2\sigma(x)$.

::: {#cell-fig-predict-noise .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x, y = datasets.heteroscedastic_noise(n=250, seed=0)
mu = np.polyval(np.polyfit(x, y, 5), x)         # the mean model
resid = y - mu                                   # residuals = the noise
sigma = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.polyval(np.polyfit(x, resid**2, 2), x), 1e-6, None))
const = resid.std()
print(f"constant band : 2-sigma coverage {np.mean(np.abs(resid) <= 2*const):.2f}")
print(f"sigma(x) band : 2-sigma coverage {np.mean(np.abs(resid) <= 2*sigma):.2f}")

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharey=True)
axL.fill_between(x, mu - 2*const, mu + 2*const, color=CRASH, alpha=0.18)
axL.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=INK, alpha=0.6); axL.plot(x, mu, c=INK, lw=2)
axL.set_title("one error bar (constant noise)", fontsize=12); despine(axL)
axR.fill_between(x, mu - 2*sigma, mu + 2*sigma, color=COOL, alpha=0.30)
axR.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=INK, alpha=0.6); axR.plot(x, mu, c=INK, lw=2)
axR.set_title("predicted σ(x) — the band breathes", fontsize=12); despine(axR)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
axL.set_ylabel("y")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
constant band : 2-sigma coverage 0.94
sigma(x) band : 2-sigma coverage 0.96
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A constant error bar (left) is wrong everywhere when the noise varies: too wide on the quiet left, barely enough on the loud right. Predicting sigma(x) from the squared residuals (right) makes the band breathe — tight where the world is calm, wide where it is noisy. Both reach ~95% coverage, but only the second puts the uncertainty in the right place.](04-predictive-bands_files/figure-html/fig-predict-noise-output-2.png){#fig-predict-noise width=1304 height=441}
:::
:::


In markets the noise has a name — **volatility** — and it is *predictable* because
it **clusters**: turbulent days follow turbulent days.  So "predict the noise"
becomes "forecast volatility."  A one-line causal forecast (EWMA, the RiskMetrics
estimator) already tracks it: $\sigma_t^2 = \lambda\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 +
(1-\lambda)\,r_{t-1}^2$, using only the past.

::: {#cell-fig-vol-band .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R = datasets.load_returns()
r = R["JPM"].to_numpy(); dates = R.index
lam, v = 0.94, np.empty_like(r)
v[0] = np.var(r[:20])
for t in range(1, len(r)):
    v[t] = lam * v[t - 1] + (1 - lam) * r[t - 1] ** 2   # causal: only the past
sigma_t = np.sqrt(v)
print(f"|r_t| <= 2*sigma_t coverage: {np.mean(np.abs(r) <= 2*sigma_t):.2f}  (target 0.95)")
print(f"forecast vol, calm vs crash: {np.median(sigma_t):.3f} vs {sigma_t.max():.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax.fill_between(dates, -2 * sigma_t, 2 * sigma_t, color=COOL, alpha=0.35,
                label="±2σ̂  (volatility forecast)")
ax.plot(dates, r, c=INK, lw=0.5, alpha=0.8)
mark_event(ax, pd.Timestamp("2008-09-15"), "Lehman")
mark_event(ax, pd.Timestamp("2020-03-16"), "COVID")
ax.set_ylim(-0.18, 0.18); ax.set_ylabel("JPM daily return")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=10, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
|r_t| <= 2*sigma_t coverage: 0.94  (target 0.95)
forecast vol, calm vs crash: 0.014 vs 0.095
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![JPM daily returns with a +/- 2 sigma band from a causal EWMA volatility forecast. The band balloons through the 2008-09 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID crash, and tightens in the calm mid-2010s - exactly the heteroscedastic noise the constant bar cannot represent. It still misses a few percent more days than it should: fat tails, which Gaussianizing the residuals (Chapter 2) would absorb.](04-predictive-bands_files/figure-html/fig-vol-band-output-2.png){#fig-vol-band width=1305 height=416}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## Why It Under-Covers
A good volatility forecast still lets ~6% of days breach the 2σ band instead of
5%: returns are **fat-tailed**, and a Gaussian 2σ rule under-counts the extremes.
Gaussianize the standardized residuals first (the [Chapter 2](../gaussianization/index.qmd)
move) and the coverage snaps back — the noise model handles *when*, Gaussianization
handles *how heavy*.
:::

## Epistemic · Ensembles

A different question: does the model **know**?  Refit it on resampled data and you
get an **ensemble**.  Where the members agree, the model is confident; where they
fan out, it is guessing — and that happens exactly where it has seen little data.

::: {#cell-fig-ensemble .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x, y = datasets.heteroscedastic_gap(n=60, seed=0)
xs = np.linspace(-5, 5, 300)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ens = []
for _ in range(40):
    idx = rng.integers(0, x.size, x.size)
    ens.append(np.polyval(np.polyfit(x[idx], y[idx], 5), xs))
ens = np.array(ens)
em, esd = ens.mean(0), ens.std(0)
gap = (xs > -1) & (xs < 1)
print(f"epistemic sd in data: {esd[(np.abs(xs) < 3) & ~gap].mean():.2f}")
print(f"epistemic sd in gap : {esd[gap].mean():.2f}   ← wider where data is sparse")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
ax.fill_between(xs, em - 2 * esd, em + 2 * esd, color=plotting.PALETTE["green"], alpha=0.25)
for member in ens[:12]:
    ax.plot(xs, member, c=plotting.PALETTE["green"], lw=0.6, alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(xs, em, c=INK, lw=2); ax.scatter(x, y, s=18, c=INK, zorder=5)
ax.axvspan(-1, 1, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08)        # the data gap
ax.set_ylim(-2.2, 2.2); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
epistemic sd in data: 0.04
epistemic sd in gap : 0.07   ← wider where data is sparse
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![An ensemble of degree-5 fits on bootstrap resamples. The members agree tightly where data is dense and fan out over the central gap and beyond the data - the model correctly reports where it has seen nothing. Unlike aleatoric noise, this band shrinks as you add data.](04-predictive-bands_files/figure-html/fig-ensemble-output-2.png){#fig-ensemble width=1064 height=440}
:::
:::


Stack the two and you have an honest predictive band:
$\sigma^2(x) = \sigma_{\text{aleatoric}}^2(x) + \sigma_{\text{epistemic}}^2(x)$ —
the noise that will never go away plus the doubt that more data would cure.

## The Capstone — One Machine, Three Uses

The course in one figure.  A single invertible map $T$: **forward** it
Gaussianizes, and the gap it closes is the dependence we *measure*
([Ch. 1](../dependence/index.qmd)) and *remove*
([Ch. 4](../fairness/index.qmd)); **backward** it generates, sampling the simple
law and inverting to the real, dependent world to *propagate* (this chapter).

::: {#cell-fig-capstone .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch  # noqa: F401  (kept for parity)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1400
f = rng.standard_t(5, n)
a = 0.85 * f + 0.35 * rng.standard_t(5, n)
b = 0.85 * f + 0.35 * rng.standard_t(5, n)
Xd = np.column_stack([a, b]); Xd = (Xd - Xd.mean(0)) / Xd.std(0)
Z = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xd)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 5.2))
axL = fig.add_axes([0.04, 0.18, 0.30, 0.66])
axC = fig.add_axes([0.37, 0.0, 0.26, 1.0]); axC.axis("off")
axR = fig.add_axes([0.66, 0.18, 0.30, 0.66])

axL.scatter(Xd[:, 0], Xd[:, 1], s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("DATA space", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axL, 0.5, -0.13, "correlated · fat-tailed")
axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([]); despine(axL)

axR.scatter(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], s=7, c=plotting.PALETTE["green"], alpha=0.35,
            edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title("GAUSSIAN space", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.13, "independent · spherical")
axR.set_xticks([]); axR.set_yticks([]); despine(axR)

axC.annotate("", xy=(0.95, 0.62), xytext=(0.05, 0.62),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", lw=2.4, color=INK))
axC.text(0.5, 0.70, "forward:  z = T(x)", ha="center", fontsize=12,
         family="monospace", fontweight="bold")
axC.text(0.5, 0.58, "MEASURE (Ch.1) · REMOVE (Ch.4)", ha="center", fontsize=9,
         color=COOL, fontweight="bold")
axC.annotate("", xy=(0.05, 0.36), xytext=(0.95, 0.36),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", lw=2.4, color=WARM))
axC.text(0.5, 0.28, "backward:  x = T⁻¹(z)", ha="center", fontsize=12,
         family="monospace", fontweight="bold")
axC.text(0.5, 0.16, "PROPAGATE (Ch.3)", ha="center", fontsize=9, color=WARM,
         fontweight="bold")
axC.text(0.5, 0.92, "One machine, three uses", ha="center", fontsize=13,
         fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Measure · remove · propagate are three directions of one change of variables. Forward: data → Gaussian (the distortion is the dependence). Backward: Gaussian → data (sampling the real joint).](04-predictive-bands_files/figure-html/fig-capstone-output-1.png){#fig-capstone width=1459 height=647}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Whole Course, One Line
**Claim only what your evidence justifies.**  The Gaussian is the least-committal
joint distribution; what $T$ removes or generates is *exactly* the dependence in
the data — nothing assumed, nothing discarded.  Signal (measure), neutrality
(remove), and risk (propagate) are one operation, read three ways.
:::

The hands-on [labs](labs/index.qmd) propagate a real portfolio to its tail risk.
